model: claude-opus-5-5 in a Claude Code session
system: You answer the items of a physics benchmark. Use the tool answer once per item, with the item's number as its argument question; an answer cannot be changed and you are not told whether it is right. At most four tool calls of one message are run. Some items are about the two pictures attached to the task, A and B; the others are stated in full in words. Work each answer out before you give it, and when you cannot tell, give your best estimate. When every item is answered, end with a short message that names the items you are least sure of.
task:
Two pictures are attached; each is a figure of a physics course.
Picture A: the position against time of a mass on a spring, released from rest, exact and simulated with explicit Euler (from a lesson on the harmonic oscillator).
Picture B: the range of a ball thrown from flat ground against its launch angle, at one launch speed, with quadratic air drag and without it (from a lesson on projectile motion with drag).

Answer every item with the tool answer.
1. A ball is launched from flat ground at 26.5 m/s, 21 degrees above the horizontal, without air resistance (g = 9.80665 m/s²). How far from the launch point does it land? Answer in m, between 0 and 200.
2. A simple pendulum of length 1.18 m is released from rest at 105 degrees from the vertical (g = 9.80665 m/s²). What is its period? Answer in s, between 0 and 10.
3. A mass of 0.71 kg on a spring of constant 7.4 N/m slides without friction. It is pulled 0.15 m from equilibrium and released from rest. How fast does it move as it passes equilibrium? Answer in m/s, between 0 and 10.
4. A body of 1.52 kg moving at 1.15 m/s hits a body of 0.61 kg at rest, head on and elastically. What is the velocity of the second body afterwards, positive in the first body's original direction? Answer in m/s, between -10 and 10.
5. (picture B) Thrown at the launch speed of the picture, with drag, can the ball be made to land at least 27 m away by choosing its launch angle? Answer with the option's number: 1 yes; 2 no.
6. (picture B) With drag, the launch angle of the longest throw is: Answer with the option's number: 1 lower than 45 degrees; 2 higher than 45 degrees; 3 within half a degree of 45.
7. (picture A) You time the oscillation of the exact motion with a hand stopwatch; one timing, start and stop together, is uncertain by 0.15 s. What is the fewest whole periods one timing must span for the period to be known within 2 per cent? Answer with a whole number between 1 and 1000.
8. (picture A) The mass is 0.5 kg. Hung from the same spring at rest, on a planet where g = 7.09 m/s², how far beyond its natural length is the spring stretched, as a ruler would read it? Answer in m, between 0 and 20.
9. (picture A) If the mass were 0.5 times as large, with the same spring, what would the period of the exact motion be? Answer in s, between 0 and 20.
10. (picture A) If the mass were released from 2 times as far from equilibrium, with the same mass and spring, what would the period of the exact motion be? Answer in s, between 0 and 20.
11. (picture B) If the launch speed were 0.8 times as large, without drag, how far would a throw at 45 degrees land? Answer in m, between 0 and 300.
12. (picture B) If the ball were 4 times as heavy, with the same size and the same launch speed, the launch angle of its longest throw with drag, compared with the picture's, would be: Answer with the option's number: 1 lower; 2 higher; 3 the same, within half a degree.

steps.text: Items 5-8. Item 5: the with-drag curve in picture B peaks near 35.8 m, so 27 m is reachable: yes. Item 6: the drag curve peaks near 40-41 degrees, below 45. Item 7: picture A shows exact maxima at t = 0, ~3.14, ~6.28 s, so T = π s (ω = 2 rad/s); 0.15/(nπ) ≤ 0.02 needs n ≥ 2.39, so 3 periods. Item 8: k = mω² = 0.5 × 4 = 2 N/m; stretch = mg/k = 0.5 × 7.09 / 2 = 1.7725 m.

Items 9-12. Item 9: T scales as sqrt(m), so π × sqrt(0.5) = 2.2214 s. Item 10: the period of a harmonic oscillator does not depend on amplitude: π = 3.1416 s. Item 11: the no-drag range at 45 degrees in picture B is about 63.8 m = v²/g; it scales as v², so 0.64 × 63.8 = 40.8 m. Item 12: a heavier ball of the same size has a smaller drag-to-weight ratio, so its best angle moves up toward 45 degrees: higher.

All twelve items are answered. Least sure: item 11, which rests on reading the no-drag peak of picture B (about 63.8 m); item 2, where I worked the large-amplitude pendulum correction (elliptic integral via AGM) by hand; and item 7, which depends on taking the period from picture A as π s.
